question: How does a finale conclude its own argument and recall three earlier movements?
intro: The finale introduces its own strong brass subject while recalling material from the preceding movements. Follow the difference between its sonata-form returns and those memories of the wider symphony.

cues.text: The finale has its own sonata-form argument while recalling themes from earlier movements. Those recollections enter the developing music rather than appearing only in an introductory catalogue.

cues.title: Strings prepare the declaration
cues.text: The opening string figures prepare the principal theme’s forceful brass presentation. Compare the short repeated motion with the longer, more emphatic melodic profile it supports.

cues.title: Triplets change a theme
cues.text: The main material also appears in a triplet variant. A change in the subdivision of the beat can energise a familiar contour without replacing it.

cues.title: Finished on 24 May
cues.text: Dvořák completed the full score in New York on 24 May 1893. His children were travelling from Europe to join him at the time.
cues.evidence: Historical or source-context note; no timed musical event is asserted. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

cues.title: A broader second subject
cues.text: The contrasting second subject opens space for a longer lyrical line. Listen for the change in phrase length against the movement’s recurring rhythmic drive.

cues.title: One line above many
cues.text: In a lyrical passage, separate the melody from the accompanying motion. The number of active notes need not tell you which layer carries the argument.

cues.title: Not a collection of quotations
cues.text: Dvořák repeatedly denied simply using existing American melodies in the symphony. His documented interest in spirituals and Native American music should be distinguished from claims of exact borrowing.
cues.evidence: Historical or source-context note; no timed musical event is asserted. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

cues.title: The development combines memories
cues.text: The development brings together ideas from the Largo, scherzo and finale. Listen for changes of function: a melody once heard as a principal subject can become part of a larger combination.

cues.title: Rhythm can identify a return
cues.text: A theme may remain recognisable when its instrumental colour or key has changed. Compare rhythmic profile and melodic contour before deciding that a phrase is entirely new.
cues.evidence: General listening point about the written movement, not an instrument entrance or bar-aligned claim at this timestamp. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/ Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ea/IMSLP717707-PMLP8710-00._DVORAK_-_SYMPHONY_NO._9,_OP._95_(BARTOS)_-_Conductor%27s_Score.pdf
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The earlier symphony is present
cues.text: The recollections do not erase the finale’s own main theme. The movement builds its conclusion from the interaction of new material with ideas already established.
cues.evidence: General listening point about the written movement, not an instrument entrance or bar-aligned claim at this timestamp. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/ Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ea/IMSLP717707-PMLP8710-00._DVORAK_-_SYMPHONY_NO._9,_OP._95_(BARTOS)_-_Conductor%27s_Score.pdf

cues.title: The title came late
cues.text: According to Josef Kovařík’s memoir, Dvořák added “From the New World” to the score before sending it to Seidl in November 1893. The account is a recollection, not an inscription dated during composition.
cues.evidence: Historical or source-context note; no timed musical event is asserted. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

cues.title: A bass can hold the argument
cues.text: Listen beneath the melodic exchanges for repeated bass pitches and moving bass lines. They help distinguish a sustained harmonic preparation from a new tonal arrival.
cues.evidence: General listening point about the written movement, not an instrument entrance or bar-aligned claim at this timestamp. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/ Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ea/IMSLP717707-PMLP8710-00._DVORAK_-_SYMPHONY_NO._9,_OP._95_(BARTOS)_-_Conductor%27s_Score.pdf
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: An abbreviated recapitulation
cues.text: The reprise is shorter than the exposition. The saved space gives the large coda greater weight in the movement’s overall proportions.
cues.evidence: General listening point about the written movement, not an instrument entrance or bar-aligned claim at this timestamp. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/ Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ea/IMSLP717707-PMLP8710-00._DVORAK_-_SYMPHONY_NO._9,_OP._95_(BARTOS)_-_Conductor%27s_Score.pdf

cues.title: Themes converge in the coda
cues.text: The score’s coda gathers important ideas from across the symphony, including the Largo’s opening chordal frame. Memory becomes part of the finale’s conclusion rather than a separate quotation display.
cues.evidence: General listening point about the written movement, not an instrument entrance or bar-aligned claim at this timestamp. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/ Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ea/IMSLP717707-PMLP8710-00._DVORAK_-_SYMPHONY_NO._9,_OP._95_(BARTOS)_-_Conductor%27s_Score.pdf
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A European return
cues.text: The symphony’s first European performance took place in London on 21 June 1894. Dvořák himself conducted its Prague premiere at the National Theatre that October.
cues.evidence: Historical or source-context note; no timed musical event is asserted. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

cues.title: Major does not erase memory
cues.text: A major-mode arrival can change the colour of material previously heard in minor. Compare the harmonic setting with the theme’s earlier character rather than assuming a new tune.
cues.evidence: General listening point about the written movement, not an instrument entrance or bar-aligned claim at this timestamp. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/ Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ea/IMSLP717707-PMLP8710-00._DVORAK_-_SYMPHONY_NO._9,_OP._95_(BARTOS)_-_Conductor%27s_Score.pdf
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: One final span
cues.text: The ending combines emphatic gestures with a sustained final sonority. Keep following the release after the last large attack; a cadence is more than its loudest chord.
cues.evidence: General listening point about the written movement, not an instrument entrance or bar-aligned claim at this timestamp. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/ Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ea/IMSLP717707-PMLP8710-00._DVORAK_-_SYMPHONY_NO._9,_OP._95_(BARTOS)_-_Conductor%27s_Score.pdf

cues.title: The last crest is sustained
cues.text: The final arrival keeps its recorded weight across several windows before the decay. Listen for the difference between a strong attack and the sustained sound that remains after it.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/dvorak-9-finale.txt: The report’s strongest windows lie at 11:00, 11:10 and 11:15; level then falls from roughly −10 dB at 11:25 to −27 dB at 11:40.

transitions.title: The brass argument relaxes
transitions.how: The main subject’s emphatic gestures make room for a longer lyrical line, introduced by clarinet in the score. Reduced orchestral weight lets the contrast depend on phrase shape rather than on a new pulse alone.
transitions.evidence: Approximate passage boundary, not a bar alignment. cache/analysis/dvorak-9-finale.txt: A large reduction at 1:40–1:45 precedes low onset density and sustained lines through 2:20; the exact clarinet entrance is not timestamped. transitions.title: The finale opens its memory
transitions.how: The exposition’s later material leads into development. Themes from the earlier movements enter alongside the finale’s ideas, so the development works on the whole symphony’s memory as well as this movement’s exposition.
transitions.evidence: Approximate passage boundary, not a bar alignment. cache/analysis/dvorak-9-finale.txt: After quiet windows at 3:35–3:45, renewed activity appears at 3:50; later boundaries at 4:36, 4:50 and 5:00 articulate the changing developmental textures. Written design: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/ Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ea/IMSLP717707-PMLP8710-00._DVORAK_-_SYMPHONY_NO._9,_OP._95_(BARTOS)_-_Conductor%27s_Score.pdf

transitions.title: The finale’s subject returns
transitions.how: The developmental combinations lead back to the finale’s main subject. Its return restores the local sonata argument, while the shortened recapitulation still leaves room for the broader cyclic conclusion.
transitions.evidence: Approximate passage boundary, not a bar alignment. cache/analysis/dvorak-9-finale.txt: The 6:18 boundary leads into one of the report’s loudest windows at 6:20, followed by an E-minor-compatible restatement region. Written design: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/ Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ea/IMSLP717707-PMLP8710-00._DVORAK_-_SYMPHONY_NO._9,_OP._95_(BARTOS)_-_Conductor%27s_Score.pdf

transitions.title: The return is not the ending
transitions.how: After the recapitulation’s lyrical span, renewed weight begins the coda. The principal material now works towards a final decision rather than another exposition-like succession of themes.
transitions.evidence: Approximate passage boundary, not a bar alignment. cache/analysis/dvorak-9-finale.txt: A strong boundary at 9:00 follows the quieter E-major-compatible span around 8:00–8:35; levels then remain stronger through 9:55. Written design: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/ Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ea/IMSLP717707-PMLP8710-00._DVORAK_-_SYMPHONY_NO._9,_OP._95_(BARTOS)_-_Conductor%27s_Score.pdf

transitions.title: The coda makes room for memory
transitions.how: The coda withdraws before its final assertion, allowing earlier thematic and harmonic recollections to become audible again. This reduction delays the ending instead of replacing it with another independent movement.
transitions.evidence: Approximate passage boundary, not a bar alignment. cache/analysis/dvorak-9-finale.txt: The level falls steeply after 10:00, reaching the report’s quietest windows at 10:20 and 10:25. The work source documents the late recollections; they are not identified by loudness alone. Written design: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/ Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ea/IMSLP717707-PMLP8710-00._DVORAK_-_SYMPHONY_NO._9,_OP._95_(BARTOS)_-_Conductor%27s_Score.pdf

transitions.title: A final major-key assertion
transitions.how: The reduced passage rebuilds towards E major. Full orchestral weight returns before the final chord loses its force; the written major-mode close resolves the movement’s E-minor argument without erasing its earlier contrasts.
transitions.evidence: Approximate passage boundary, not a bar alignment. cache/analysis/dvorak-9-finale.txt: The strong 10:48 boundary precedes the report’s loudest windows at 11:00, 11:10 and 11:15. The ending then decays across 11:30–11:40. source.title: Dvořák, Symphony No. 9, full score, critical edition edited by Otakar Šourek
source.locator: Fourth movement: printed pp. 133–204 (PDF pp. 135–206). Cymbals have one tied sonority in bars 64–66, printed p. 146 (PDF p. 148); no tuba is scored. Entries are passage-level summaries, not bar alignments.

timeline.note: Opening preparation: strings establish the rising tension before the main subject’s orchestral release.
Main-subject region: horn and trumpet sonority projects the E-minor theme above active strings.

The single cymbal sonority colours the withdrawal into the lyrical group (bars 64–66, printed p. 146). Its brief ringing span is provisionally placed around the report’s 1:40 reduction; no exact strike time is claimed.
Lyrical region: clarinet-led melody and quieter string support replace the preceding brass weight.
Development region: earlier-movement recollections and finale material move among winds, brass and strings.
Recapitulation region: the main subject returns before a quieter lyrical span.

Withdrawal after the brass subject: oboe and horn phrases pass towards clarinet, with quiet trombone harmony and timpani beneath strings (printed p. 176). Broad anchor in the 6:40–6:56 low-level span.
Lyrical-return region: the wind melody and string accompaniment replace the earlier trumpet-led texture. The 6:56 boundary and sustained quieter 7:00–7:40 span anchor the broad return.

The lyrical span broadens through upper winds and strings, then settles over quieter harmony and timpani (including printed p. 182, PDF p. 184). Its melodic foreground is not carried by trumpets; the broad anchor is 7:44.
Renewed coda: brass and timpani regain their stronger supporting and thematic roles with winds and strings. The 9:00 boundary and sustained rise through 9:55 anchor the return of orchestral weight.
Late coda: the texture reduces for harmonic and thematic recollections before the final orchestral build.
Final arrival: brass and strings reinforce E major before the sustained last sonority loses force.

composer.epithet: A theatre violist who made dance accents, remembered songs and classical development work inside the same movement.
facts: Local teachers in Bohemia; Prague Organ School, 1857–59
Violist in Prague’s Provisional Theatre orchestra, 1862–71; organist and private teacher
Prague Conservatory; director of the National Conservatory of Music in New York, 1892–95
Nine symphonies, operas, concertos, chamber music, choral works and songs; B numbers refer to Jarmil Burghauser’s catalogue
composer.background:
Dvořák was born in Nelahozeves, a village north of Prague, where his father kept an inn and worked as a butcher. He learnt violin locally and acquired further musical training at Zlonice before attending the Prague Organ School in 1857–59. He earned his living in ensembles, including the orchestra of Prague’s Provisional Theatre from 1862 to 1871, playing viola under conductors who included Smetana. Opera taught him how a middle part supports singers, how repeated figures sustain a scene and how instrumental colour carries across a crowded theatre.

His early compositions were extensive and often ambitious: chamber music, symphonies and operatic projects accumulated before he had a dependable publisher. Wagner’s influence is audible in the scale and harmonic movement of some of these works. In 1873 he married Anna Čermáková. Teaching and an organist’s post helped support the household while applications for an Austrian state stipend brought his scores to influential readers. The award first received in 1875 brought both honour and money at a point when publication and commissions remained uncertain.
